title: To the land of a just king
hook: the Prophet ﷺ sends some to Abyssinia, where a king rules who wrongs no one (sirah)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ta-Ha, the page Umar read after his sister stood her ground. Your line was: the page turned him.

A leader who can't protect his people has a hard choice. He can tell them to hold on. He can tell them to fight. Or he can tell them to leave. Ibn Ishaq says that when the Prophet, peace be upon him, saw what his companions were suffering, and that he could not shield them, he pointed them across the sea, to Abyssinia. Not because the land was Muslim; it wasn't. Because of the man who ruled it. Today: hijrah.
screen: `HOLD ON, FIGHT, OR LEAVE?` → `ACROSS THE SEA.` → `BECAUSE OF THE KING.`

segments.voice: Here is what Ibn Ishaq has him say, in paraphrase: if you go to Abyssinia, you'll find a king there under whom no one is wronged. It is a land of truthfulness, until God makes a way out for you from what you're in. Look at what he praises. Not the king's religion; he is a Christian, ruling a Christian land. Not his wealth or his army. Justice. The Prophet trusted his people to a ruler of another faith because that ruler was fair. So some of the Muslims went. Ibn Ishaq calls it the first emigration in Islam, the first hijrah, before the later one to Medina. Among those who went, he names Uthman ibn Affan and his wife Ruqayyah, the Prophet's own daughter. This wasn't sending strangers away. He sent his child. Umm Salamah, who went too, later remembered what they found. In her report in Musnad Ahmad, she says they came to the best of neighbors, were safe in their faith, and worshipped God without being harmed or hearing anything they hated. Safe in their faith, in someone else's country. Tomorrow, Quraysh come after them. For now, notice the picture: the first hijrah was Muslims running for safety to the court of a just king.
screen: `NO ONE IS WRONGED THERE.` · `HE PRAISES JUSTICE, NOT RELIGION.` · `HE SENT HIS OWN DAUGHTER.` · `SAFE IN THEIR FAITH, FAR FROM HOME.`

segments.voice: Think of fairness from someone who owed you nothing: a person outside your circle, of another faith or background, who held the rules level when tilting them would have been easy, like an honest official, a referee who called it straight against the home crowd, a landlord who gave back the whole deposit. Notice exactly what they did, and what it might have cost them. Then say your thanks quietly, naming the fair thing, and if you pray, you can pray for them.
Hijrah. The Prophet sends companions to Abyssinia, the first emigration in Islam, to a king who, he says, rules so that no one is wronged. Today's word.
Your line: a just king. Justice, not religion, was the reason he gave. That's day seven hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Muslims know this as the emigration to Abyssinia (al-Habashah), told in sirah lessons as the community's first hijrah, and the Negus is remembered with honor for sheltering them.

chat.says: Why did the Prophet send Muslims to Abyssinia, a Christian land?
options: Because its king was just; he said no one is wronged under him.
Because Abyssinia's army had promised to fight Quraysh for them.
Because the leaders of Mecca ordered all new believers to leave.
chat.meaning: Ibn Ishaq has him say there is a king in Abyssinia under whom no one is wronged. He praised the king's justice, not his religion.

hijrah.meaning: emigration for the sake of faith

Abyssinia.meaning: the land across the sea, ruled by a just king

Uthman ibn Affan.meaning: Ruqayyah's husband, among the first emigrants

Umm Salamah.meaning: an emigrant who later told what they found

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the first emigration to Abyssinia: a king under whom none is wronged, a land of truthfulness; Uthman and Ruqayyah among the emigrants)
Musnad Ahmad 1740 (Umm Salamah: in Abyssinia, the best of neighbors; safe in their religion)

notes: The Prophet's words about the king are paraphrased from Ibn Ishaq; confirm.
'The first emigration in Islam' is attributed to Ibn Ishaq; confirm the wording there.
Musnad Ahmad 1740 number cited from memory (Umm Salamah's long report); confirm. The same report carries Ja'far's speech (day 743).
Umm Salamah's presence on the first emigration vs. a later party: the script says only that she went too. Confirm.

The Negus is described as a Christian ruling a Christian land, with no claim about his later faith; Muslim tradition holds he later accepted Islam (the Prophet prayed the funeral prayer for him). A Keeper may want this noted on a later day.
